claims.text: The controlled starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state without secondary phases.
Atomic short-range order governs the balance among deformation behavior, hardness, and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Slow cooling increases short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid quenching freezes in greater atomic disorder and minimizes short-range order in CoCrFeNiTi.
Increased short-range order produces localized lattice distortions.
Short-range order can create additional resistance to dislocation glide.
Obstacles to slip determine yield strength at small plastic strains.
Slow-cooled CoCrFeNiTi with greater short-range order will have higher hardness and compressive yield strength than rapidly quenched material.
Greater short-range order will reduce plastic strain and ductility.
Rapidly quenched samples will retain a more homogeneous solid solution than slow-cooled samples.
Fewer barriers to dislocation glide in rapidly quenched samples will produce greater ductility and machinability.
Conventionally processed equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a moderate inherent short-range-order level, moderate hardness and strength, and good plasticity.
Atom-probe tomography or fluctuation electron microscopy can quantify the relevant short-range order.
The proposed comparison uses room-temperature and 600 °C compression at approximately 10^-3 s^-1 and nominally up to 10% compressive strain.
The comparison is intended to hold composition, grain structure, dimensions, loading protocol, and phase constitution constant while changing only cooling rate.
Accurate experimental control and quantification of short-range order are challenging.
Residual stresses may contribute to the measured mechanical differences independently of short-range order.
A measured short-range-order difference without the predicted increase in hardness and strength and decrease in plasticity would falsify the proposed governing relationship.

contradictions.description: The mechanical tests are nominally limited to 10% compressive strain, but strain to failure is listed as a measurement. Strain to failure cannot be determined for specimens that remain intact at the stated test limit.
